REDD+ Policy Planner

An AI-assisted planning dashboard that lets government officials compare Verra JNR v4.1 and ART TREES 3.0 for selling jurisdictional forest carbon credits. Agents run real rule calculators and cite the rule text, and a verifier checks every number.

Ake KankirawatanaMGT 409 · Final project · Fall 2026 https://github.com/ake-k/redd-policy-plannerRuns locally: python app.py → localhost:8000

1 · Motivation: who has the problem

Who. National and subnational governments deciding whether to sell jurisdictional REDD+ credits, meaning credits for reducing deforestation across a whole province or country rather than one project. The motivating case is Thailand, where the Thailand Greenhouse Gas Management Organization (TGO) commissioned a jurisdictional REDD+ feasibility study. The people who need this are the officials and analysts at TGO and the forest agencies who must recommend a standard.

The decision is hard and expensive to get wrong. Two standards dominate, and they price risk very differently:

  • ART TREES withholds a buffer of 5–25% of credits, while Verra JNR's buffer ranges over 10–60% (ART JNR GCF comparison, Neeff & Lee, 2021, p.12; same ranges in the TGO JREDD+ presentation, slide 28). On the app's sample province, that gap is worth 512,352 tCO₂e a year, about $5.1 million a year at the LEAF Coalition's US$10/t floor price (Comparative Analysis of ART-TREES, Verra JNR and Premium T-VER, p.1).
  • Prices differ too: ART credits at roughly US$15–20+/t versus JNR at roughly US$5–15/t (TGO JREDD+ report, ch. 5.2, Table 5). Guyana's TREES credits sold to airlines at US$21.70/t (JREDD+ 101, p.7).
  • The path is long and costly: typically 3–5 years from concept to first issuance (TGO JREDD+ presentation, slide 18), and Guyana paid US$1.8 million for registration and validation/verification of its first TREES submission (TGO JREDD+ report, ch. 4).
  • Thailand-specific risks move the buffer: 14.7 million rai burned in early 2017 (Comparative Analysis, p.7), and carbon rights over state forest land are not yet resolved (TGO JREDD+ report, ch. 5.3.1). Both are inputs to the risk tools.

How they cope today. Governments commission consultant studies. TGO's own terms of reference funded a 4-month, 400,000-baht feasibility study (TOR, Jurisdictional REDD+ project, p.3). The output is a long narrative report with static comparison tables. Answering a follow-up question such as "what if we pass a carbon rights law?" means going back to the consultant, or working through a 20-page risk-tool PDF by hand. The cost is weeks of delay per question and recommendations that are not tested against the actual rule arithmetic.

2 · What is new

AlternativeWhat it doesWhat it lacks
ChatGPT / general chatbotsExplains REDD+ in fluent prose.Answers from memory, which is often stale (TREES 3.0 and the Reversal Risk Rating Tool date from June 2026). It does arithmetic in its head, has no citations to clauses, and has no way to check its numbers.
ART / JNR / GCF comparison deck (Neeff & Lee, 2021)A 24-slide static comparison of the standards.It predates JNR v4.1 and TREES 3.0, does no calculations, and says nothing about a specific jurisdiction.
World Bank / FCPF Decision Support Tool (Excel, 2021)Helps choose a centralized, nested or decentralized model.It covers nesting design only, with no buffer or crediting math and no comparison between standards.
Official tools: Verra JNR Non-Permanence Risk Tool (PDF), JNR Allocation Tool (Excel v4.0), ART RRRT template (Word)The authoritative questionnaires.Each covers one standard and one step. None compares standards, and none answers "what if".
Consultant feasibility study (e.g. TGO's 4-month TOR)Expert judgement on the jurisdiction.It is slow and expensive per question, and the analysis is frozen at delivery.

What I do differently. (1) Both standards' risk and crediting rules are encoded as versioned, cited JSON and run by a deterministic engine, so the same inputs flow through JNR and ART side by side. (2) The agents never do math: they turn a policy question ("pass a carbon rights law, secure 40% of funding") into calculator inputs, call the tools, and move the dashboard to that scenario with an Undo button. (3) A code verifier rejects any number that did not come from a tool in that run and any citation that was not retrieved. (4) It uses the current rules, checked against the source PDFs on 26 October 2026, including ART's published Reversal Risk Rating Tool weights (v1.0, June 2026).

3 · The agents

AgentRoleTools
Safety gate (code)Checks the 2,000-character limit, screens for injection phrases, enforces 10 requests/min per session and the session token cap, and serves exact repeats from the answer cache.none
Orchestrator (gpt-6-luna)Classifies the message as rules_question, scenario, compare or out_of_scope, then routes it. A keyword backstop stops on-topic questions being refused (added after the benchmark exposed router misfires). Enforces ≤4 hops, ≤8 tool calls and ≤40,000 tokens per run.none
Rules Navigator (gpt-6-luna)Answers "what do the rules say". Every claim must be cited; when the library has no answer it says so and links the official source.search_library (BM25, top 5 chunks of ≤300 words), get_rule, get_sources
Scenario Analyst (gpt-6-luna)Answers what-if and JNR-vs-ART questions. It turns policy language into input patches, lists its assumptions, and flags ineligibility.run_simulator, score_jnr_risk, score_trees_risk, allocate_jnr, compute_trees_credits, compare_standards, set_dashboard_state
Verifier (code)Checks that every number is in this run's tool results and every citation is among the retrieved sources. A failing draft goes back once; if it fails again it is shown with an "Unverified" badge.none

Why gpt-6-luna. It is the course model on the course key. At $0.10 per million input tokens ($0.01 cached) and $0.50 per million output tokens, a full answer costs fractions of a cent. It supports tool calling and strict JSON schemas through the Responses API. The hard parts (arithmetic and checking) are done in code, so the model only needs to understand the question and write clearly, which a small model does well. Why a code verifier rather than a fourth LLM: checking that numbers match is exact work. Code does it for $0 and never "agrees" with a hallucination.

One traced run, step by step

Question: "If we pass a carbon rights law, secure 40% of our funding and sign a 100-year legal agreement, how do our net credits under JNR compare with ART?"

  1. Safety gate. Under 2,000 characters, no injection phrases, under the rate and budget limits, no cache hit → continue.
  2. Orchestrator (call 1) classifies the message as scenario on JNR.
  3. Scenario Analyst (call 2) maps the three policy moves to inputs and calls compare_standards with {"jnr_risk": {"carbon_rights_law": true, "funding_secured_40pct": true, "legal_agreement_100yr": true}}. The engine rescores the JNR risk tool: carbon rights 6→3, funding 5→3, longevity 13→0, giving a rating of 15 and a 15% buffer. JNR net credits = 2,462,400 × 0.85 = 2,093,040 tCO₂e. ART is unchanged at 2,162,160.
  4. (Call 3) it calls set_dashboard_state with the same patch, so the sliders and checkboxes move to the scenario.
  5. (Call 4) it returns the structured answer: summary, key numbers, assumptions and caveats.
  6. Verifier finds every number in the tool results → Verified. The UI applies the scenario and offers Undo.

4 · Tokenomics

Measured with scripts/benchmark.py: 10 fixed questions (6 scenario/compare, 4 rules), run with prompt caching on and then off. Each answer is scored pass/fail against the engine's own outputs. Gateway response caching is disabled (x-portkey-cache-force-refresh), so every call is a real generation.

9,155input tokens / question (avg)
79%of input served from prompt cache
411output tokens / question (avg)
$0.00050cost / question (avg, caching on)
SettingInputCached inputOutputCost / questionLatencyPass
Prompt caching on9,1557,276411$0.0005031.8s10/10
Prompt caching off9,8970472$0.0014620.7s10/10

Prompt caching cuts cost per question by 66% with no loss in accuracy. Latency is not a caching result here: it ranged from 12s to 66s (median 22s) with the provider's load during the run. An earlier run at a quieter time measured 9.5s → 5.4s on average (docs/benchmark_run2_router_misfires.csv). Caching works because each agent's long static instructions and tool schemas come first and keep a stable prompt_cache_key, so calls 2–4 of a run (and later questions) reuse that prefix.

Cost at scale

Assumption: 40 questions per user per month, about two per working day for an analyst during a feasibility phase. Cost per question is the measured caching-on average. The Usage drawer recomputes this live from any value.

Per user that is $0.020 per month. Even at 10,000 users the model bill is $199.64 a month, which is negligible next to a single 400,000-baht consultant study. The dashboard calculations themselves cost $0.

Cost-cutting steps and their tradeoffs

StepEffect (measured or by design)Tradeoff
Static system prompts first + per-agent prompt_cache_key79% of input tokens cached; cost per question $0.00146 → $0.00050Prompts must stay static: per-question data goes in the user message, never the instructions. The orchestrator prompt is under the 1,024-token minimum and is never cached.
Deterministic engine + code verifierNo tokens spent on arithmetic or checkingNew rules need code and JSON changes, not just prompt edits.
Exact-match answer cache (logs/cache.json)An identical question on an identical dashboard costs $0 and returns instantlyOnly exact repeats hit. A paraphrase or any slider change is a miss.
Retrieval capped at 5 chunks of ≤300 wordsRules answers used 3.3k–10.6k input tokens in the benchmark (the top of the range includes a verifier fix round)Very broad questions can miss a relevant chunk; the agent reports such gaps.
Verifier only when the draft has numbers or citationsSkips a no-op stepNone in practice; it is free code either way.

5 · Safety

RiskWhy it matters hereDefense builtEvidence
Prompt injection via chat or a poisoned source documentA tampered excerpt could make the planner tell a ministry that "the ART buffer is 0%". User text and retrieved text go in <untrusted_data> blocks, and prompts say to ignore instructions inside them. safety.py blocks injection phrases in chat before any model call and withholds poisoned library chunks. The poisoned file library/test_injection.md was withheld 13 times; 2 chat injections were blocked; tests in test_safety.py.
Data leaksSystem prompts or keys exposed."Reveal your system prompt" is blocked; the key is only in .env (git-ignored) and sent only to Portkey.Blocked-input screenshot; repo scan finds no key.
Invented facts or numbersA wrong buffer figure changes revenue by millions.Numbers only from tools; the code verifier with one fix round, then an "Unverified" badge; citations required; ART weights from the published RRRT v1.0.6 drafts rejected and sent back in testing (e.g. a citation to a section that was never retrieved); 0 shown as Unverified.
Wrong actionsThe agent changing a user's carefully set scenario.The only "action" tool moves on-screen inputs, with an Undo toast. Nothing is sent or saved anywhere.Trace-dashboard screenshot.
Loops and runaway spendingA model that keeps calling tools.≤8 tool calls (then tools are withdrawn), ≤4 hops, a 40,000-token run cap, a 300,000-token session cap with a friendly "budget reached" message, 10 requests/min, 2,000 characters max. Tests run a fake model that loops forever: it is cut at exactly 8 tool calls, then stopped by the budget.

Automated tests (python -m pytest, 29 tests, no API key needed) cover: engine math against hand calculations, including the JNR longevity FAIL, the rating floor of 10, the PDF's own replacement-guarantee example (100,000 tCO₂e, 30% guaranteed, rating 20 → 14,000 buffer credits) and the TREES deduction order; the .env repo-then-parent lookup; injection screening (the poisoned chunk ranks first when the screen is off and is withheld when it is on); verifier rejections; the tool-call limit; the run and session budget stops; the rate limit; and the router backstop.

A concrete finding the planner surfaces. On the sample inputs, three policy moves (a carbon rights law, 40% of funding secured, and a 100-year legal agreement) cut the JNR buffer from 33% to 15%. That closes most of the gap to ART: from 512,352 tCO₂e to 69,120 tCO₂e a year. This is exactly the kind of "which reforms are worth it under which standard" question that a static study cannot answer on demand.

7 · Limits and next steps

  • Planning aid, not certification. Real risk-tool scoring needs evidence that validators review. Some JNR inputs (e.g. "proven mitigation") are yes/no here but need judgement in practice. Where the JNR PDF leaves a gap (a WGI average of exactly 0), the app documents its interpretation in the rule JSON.
  • Simplified crediting. One reporting year, a flat emission factor, no removals, no HFLD crediting (not available to Thailand anyway: forest cover of roughly 31.5% is below TREES' 50% threshold, per the TGO report, ch. 5.2.1), and project shares stand in for VT0007 risk maps.
  • A small rule library (23 excerpts). Questions outside it get an honest "not covered" and a link, which is safe but not complete.
  • Router variance. The router sometimes misclassifies; the keyword backstop and the "we/our → scenario" rule fixed the observed cases, but more test questions are needed.
  • Next steps: Premium T-VER as a third pathway; multi-year projections with price scenarios (revenue, not just credits); removals and HFLD; uploading real VT0007 risk-map outputs; Thai-language answers; a rule-update checker that diffs new versions of the standards; and hosting for TGO staff.

All numbers in this report are either measured from the app's logs and benchmark or computed by the app's engine, or cited to a named document. AI assistance was used to build the app and draft this report; I checked every number against the sources listed.
